Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
The accident happened on a rain-slicked stretch of coastal highway, where two transport trucks and three sedans crossed paths in a violent tangle of steel and glass. Rohan was behind the wheel, gripping the steering column until his knuckles ached. The impact tore through the cabin, followed by a heavy, suffocating quiet. When the windshields settled, strangers in reflective vests and uniforms emerged from the mist, their boots crunching on safety glass. They asked him questions in rapid, clipped tones, speaking about the others he could not look at. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed; the hands that reached through his shattered window offered assistance, but their eyes carried a detached calculation that made his chest tighten. He survived the wreckage, but the man who had driven that morning was gone. In the weeks that followed, the memory refused to settle into the past. It arrived without warning, vivid and immediate, as if the steering column were still pressing against his ribs. Rohan knew what had happened, but when he tried to hold the event in his mind, the words slipped through his fingers like water. He would sit on the edge of his bed, breathing rapidly, terror rising in his throat exactly as it had in that cabin. The terror did not fade with time; it simply waited. He experienced the memories alongside a quiet unraveling of his identity, watching the same footage play behind his eyes. He did not know who he was anymore. The fisherman who used to laugh over diesel and dawn coffee was a stranger to him now. His scanning operated in parallel with his heightened alertness. Even inside his own home, where the locks were dead and the doors shut, he remained on guard. He constantly watched the windows, the stairwell, the hallway. An unusual silence in the house—a sudden absence of the refrigerator humming or the clock ticking—would send his pulse into a frantic rhythm. He was certain that silence meant something dangerous was about to happen. What frightened him most was the terror that returned each time he tried to remember, a full-bodied recall that left his hands shaking and his mind blank. He kept his experiences side by side, the memories arriving with the same physiological charge, while his body felt increasingly foreign to him. He could no longer trust his own body; a sudden shift of weight, a tight grip on a tool, made him flinch as if he had lost control of his own muscles. Rohan returned to the water, his family’s fishing skiff pulling away from the dock before dawn. The harbor became his daily setting, and the water held the triggers he could not outrun. When a delivery truck swerved and clipped the guardrail down the coastal access road, glass skittering across the asphalt, his breath caught instantly. He gripped the wheel, certain he was back in the cabin. On the boat, he kept his head on a swivel, reading the surface for rips, for floating debris, for anything that might strike without warning. When the crew fell quiet between tasks, his shoulders would knot. He avoided the town’s community center where neighbors gathered to share stories. The moment someone mentioned a husband lost to a fishing accident or a child taken by illness, Rohan would stand abruptly, muttering an excuse, and walk out. Strangers who approached him at the marina to ask about tide tables or engine repairs made his throat close. He would nod stiffly, finish the transaction, and leave. Over the months, his routine narrowed. He stopped taking charters, declined the regular supply runs to the mainland, and let the ledger books pile up. The financial strain was quiet, but it weighed on him more than the debt. It was the silence that finally pushed him to the clinic. Last Tuesday, while his skiff was tied to the buoy, the engine sputtered and died. The water went still. The crew went quiet. Rohan sat in the captain’s chair, his breath catching, the old terror flooding back. He realized he had not slept through the night in over a year, that he had stopped going to his wife’s grave because the quiet flowers reminded him of the quiet cabin. He did not know why he was afraid, only that he was. When his daughter insisted he see someone, he agreed, hoping for something to steady the tremor in his hands. He wanted to know if the terror would ever stop, and if, beneath the fear, there was still a man left to find.
